title: Beastly
full_review:
"Love is never ugly." That's the central message of "Beastly" (CBS Films), a modern take on "Beauty and the Beast" set in the fairy-tale land of high school.

Chronicling the fall and redemption of the biggest man on campus, this good-natured film offers its Facebook-generation target audience some rarely told lessons in humility, kindness and old-fashioned romance.

We first meet Kyle (Alex Pettyfer) as he's campaigning to be president of the student body. He has it all: looks, admiring ladies and lots of money. "Beautiful people get it better. That's just the way it is," Kyle tells his constituents.

His proud and equally shallow father (Peter Krause), a handsome TV anchor, backs up his son, saying, "People like people who look good. Anyone who says otherwise is dumb -- or ugly."

Enter two ladies who disagree.

The lovely Lindy (Vanessa Hudgens) may secretly pine for her new president but says, smartly, "I prefer substance over style." The eccentric Kendra (Mary-Kate Olsen), the school's resident witch, sees through Kyle's facade. After he publicly humiliates her, she sets out to teach this spoiled brat a lesson.

It's not nice to fool with Mother Nature, let alone an Olsen twin, and Kendra casts a spell, turning Kyle into a gruesome creature, giving him just one year to learn the meaning of true love and inner beauty or risk being hideous forever.

As the beast, Kyle is not the furry animal of Disney lore, but more a grunge artist covered with exotic tattoos, deep scars and metallic appliques.

Repulsed by his newly ugly son, Dad exiles him to his own luxury townhouse, where Kyle becomes a recluse. Leave it to two wise souls -- Zola (Lisa Gay Hamilton), a housekeeper with a heart of gold, and Will (Neil Patrick Harris), a blind tutor -- to teach Kyle about love, healing and helping others.

"Find someone who can see you better than you can," Zola advises.

Kyle, who hides in the shadows and now goes by the name Hunter, recalls Lindy's warmth and kindness. He rescues her from her criminal father, depositing her in his apartment in a kind of witness-protection program. Thus begins a very long (and refreshingly charming) courtship of beauty by the beast using roses and poetry.

"When I am around you, I don't feel ugly at all," Hunter/Kyle tells Lindy. She, in turn, is learning to love as she peels away his layers: "That something underneath is pure catnip for me," she says.

Based on the novel by Alex Flinn and directed by Daniel Barnz ("Phoebe in Wonderland"), "Beastly" is a warm-hearted film that sets a good example for today's teens. Thus, despite the elements listed below, it's probably acceptable for mature adolescents.

The film contains brief action violence and a few crass terms. The Catholic News Service classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
